22.title: The one who would be a steward
22.hook: Allah tells the angels He will place a steward on the earth, and they ask why (2:30)
22.howItsDone: Many Muslims understand being a khalifah on the earth as a trust: caring for creation and for one another as stewards answerable to God, and Friday sermons often return to this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: juz' 'amma, the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an, where nearly everyone begins. Your line was the ones every Muslim child knows. Day twenty-two.
screen: `JUZ' 'AMMA — THE ONES EVERY MUSLIM CHILD KNOWS.`

segments.voice: The first story doesn't start on earth at all. It starts in a conversation. God speaks to the angels, who in this verse describe themselves as hymning His praise, and tells them a plan: something new is coming. And the angels do something surprising. They ask a question. So begins camp two, the stories: the prophets, one after another, Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Yusuf, Maryam and Isa, and then the Prophet himself, peace be upon him, told in words only, the way the Qur'an tells them.
screen: `A CONVERSATION WITH THE ANGELS.` → `AND THE ANGELS ASK WHY.` → `CAMP TWO: THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, surah two, verse thirty. God says to the angels, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth.” Viceroy is Pickthall's choice. The Arabic is khalifah, and translators wrestle with it: viceroy, deputy, successor, steward. The root, kh-l-f, means to come after, to stand in for. A khalifah is someone who holds a place on another's behalf. Not the owner. The one entrusted. The later word caliph comes from it, but here it's about every human being. And the angels answer. Paraphrasing: will You place there someone who will spread corruption and shed blood, while we praise You and call You holy? Commentators are careful here: this was a question, not an objection. They wanted to understand. How could something that dangerous be the one put in charge? And God doesn't strike them down for asking. He answers, in Pickthall's words: “Surely I know that which ye know not.” Tomorrow the story shows them what He meant. This first scene sets something up. Human beings enter the story as a risk, and a trust at the same time. Capable of bloodshed. Handed the earth anyway, to look after. And the first thing that happens, before anyone has done anything, is an honest question, asked out loud, to God, and answered.

segments.voice: Let one real question come up, one you've been carrying about your life, or the world, or God: not a rhetorical one, but the kind you'd feel a little shy asking out loud, in plain words. Just sit with it; you don't have to answer it, and in the story, even the angels asked, and nobody was punished for it. If you pray, you can ask it there; if you don't, just hold it in the open, and let it breathe.
Khalifah. A steward, a deputy, one who stands in for another. The Qur'an's word, in this scene, for what a human being is here to be.
Your line: even the angels asked. Camp two has begun. Day twenty-two, done.

23.title: The names
23.hook: Allah teaches Adam the names of all things, and the angels admit they know only what they were taught (2:31–33)
23.tomorrow: The one who would not bow
23.howItsDone: Muslims often point to this passage as the root of Islam's regard for knowledge, and many teachers open lessons by recalling that God taught Adam the names.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalifah, the steward, and the angels' honest question. God's answer was: I know what you know not. Today, He shows them.

A toddler points. Dog. Ball. Moon. Every new word is a small victory, and the whole family cheers. Something enormous is happening: the world is splitting into things that can be told apart, held in the mind, talked about. Once a child can say moon, they can ask where it goes in the daytime. Now God answers the angels. And the answer isn't strength, or goodness. It's words.
screen: `A TODDLER POINTING: DOG, BALL, MOON.` → `THE WORLD SPLITS INTO THINGS.` → `THE ANSWER IS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse thirty-one, in Pickthall's words: “And He taught Adam all the names.” Then God sets the things before the angels: tell Me their names, if you're right. The angels answer honestly: “We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us.” Then Adam is asked, and he names them, one by one. That's the answer to yesterday's question. What makes this creature worth the risk? He can be taught. What were the names? The Qur'an doesn't say, and the commentators have their favorite answers. Some early authorities said everything, down to a bowl and a cooking pot. Some said the names of the angels, or of Adam's own descendants. Some later thinkers read it as the gift of language itself: the power to tell one thing from another and know it. A hadith in Bukhari, about the Day of Judgment, has people coming to Adam and listing what God gave him, and the names are on that list: He taught you the names of all things. And look at the angels. They don't bluff. They say: we only know what we were taught. To name a thing, you have to look at it long enough to tell it apart from everything else. Naming is noticing, made permanent.
screen: `HE TAUGHT ADAM ALL THE NAMES.` · `WE KNOW ONLY WHAT WE WERE TAUGHT.` · `WHAT WERE THE NAMES?` · `NAMING IS NOTICING.` · then, large: `TO NAME IS TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Look slowly around the room and name five things silently, staying with each one until you've really seen it: the color of a mug, the way the light sits on the wall. Then close your eyes and name one thing you can hear, and one you can feel. If you pray, remember who, in the story, first taught the names.
The names. What God taught Adam, and what the angels didn't know: the first gift in the human story is words.
Your line: to name is to notice. Knowing starts with looking closely. See you tomorrow.

24.title: The one who would not bow
24.hook: every angel bows to Adam except Iblis, who says he was made of fire and is better (7:11–12)
24.tomorrow: The garden and the one tree
24.howItsDone: Muslims learn this story as a warning against pride, and many recall it when they bow in prayer: the bow Iblis refused is the bow they choose, five times a day, to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the names God taught Adam, and the angels who said, we know only what we were taught. To name is to notice.
screen: `THE NAMES — TO NAME IS TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Someone new joins the team, younger, less experienced, and the boss says: they're leading this one. For some people, something goes tight in the chest. Me? Under them? Nobody says it out loud; some wouldn't admit it even to themselves. But the thought can arrive fully formed: I'm better than that. Today's story turns on that exact thought. Not a crime, not a lie: a comparison. A whole company of heavenly beings is told to bow to Adam. They all do. All but one.
screen: `SOMEONE NEW IS PUT IN CHARGE.` → `I'M BETTER THAN THAT.` → `ALL BOW BUT ONE.`

segments.voice: The scene is told several times in the Qur'an. God tells the angels to bow before Adam, and they fall down, all of them, except Iblis. God asks what kept him from bowing when he was told. Iblis answers, in Pickthall's words: “I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.” Notice his argument. It isn't about God at all. It's about material. Fire rises and shines; mud just sits there. So I'm better. It's a snob's logic. Commentators point out what he left out: the names, the knowledge, the breath God blew into Adam. He looked at the clay and stopped there. Who was Iblis? One verse says plainly that he was of the jinn, beings made of smokeless fire. Scholars differ: some say he was a jinn who'd risen to live among the angels; others, that he was an angel himself. The name? Some link it to an Arabic root for despair; others say it comes from outside Arabic. And the bow? Scholars explain it as a bow of honor to Adam, not worship, which in Islam is only for God. Islamic teaching takes pride seriously. A hadith in Muslim's collection says no one with a speck of pride in their heart will enter paradise, then defines it: pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. That's Iblis exactly. Not a monster, at first. Just someone who said: I'm better than him.

segments.voice: Think back over the last day or two for one moment when the thought appeared: I'm better than them. Don't scold yourself; just look at it, the way you'd look at a stone in your shoe, and then name one thing that person has that you don't. If you pray, you can ask for help to see it.
Iblis. The one who would not bow to Adam, because he thought fire was better than mud.
Your line: pride was the first mistake. It began with a comparison. That's day twenty-four.

25.title: The garden and the one tree
25.hook: Adam and his wife live in the garden with everything, told only to leave one tree (2:35)
25.howItsDone: Muslims read the garden story in surahs two, seven and twenty; teachers often draw from it that the permitted, halal, is wide and the forbidden is narrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Iblis, the one who would not bow, fire looking down on mud. Pride was the first mistake.

A friend lends you their apartment for a month. The fridge is full. Use the car, the pool, the good coffee, the books. Honestly, anything. Just one thing: don't open that cupboard in the hall. A hundred yeses and a single no, and it's an old joke which one ends up on people's minds that first night. Now Adam gets a home: a garden with everything in it. And one rule.
screen: `A FRIEND'S APARTMENT FOR A MONTH.` → `EVERYTHING, EXCEPT ONE CUPBOARD.` → `A GARDEN, AND ONE RULE.`

segments.voice: Surah two, verse thirty-five. God says: Adam, live in the garden, you and your wife, and in Pickthall's words, “eat ye freely (of the fruits) thereof where ye will; but come not nigh this tree lest ye become wrongdoers.” Freely, where you will. The permission is huge, and it comes first. Another surah describes the garden's promise: no hunger there, no nakedness, no thirst, no burning sun. Then the one tree. Not even don't eat, exactly: don't come near it. Keep your distance. Here's what the Qur'an doesn't say. It doesn't name Adam's wife; the name Hawwa, Eve, comes from the hadith and later tradition. It doesn't name the tree, or the fruit. There's no apple in the Qur'an; the apple came later, from outside it. Commentators guessed at wheat, or grapes, or figs, and al-Tabari concluded that we simply aren't told. Scholars even differ about the garden itself: some say it was the paradise of the hereafter, others a garden somewhere on earth. The Qur'an leaves these open and keeps its eye on one thing: a whole world of yes, and a single no. Why a no at all? One answer some scholars give: a steward, a khalifah, has to be someone who can be trusted with a limit. A life with no limits isn't a trust; it's a playground. The one tree turns the garden into a test of love, and of trust.

segments.voice: Make a quiet list of what you already have enough of: light to see by, air in this breath, a bed, something to eat later, someone who'd answer if you called. Let it get long, and notice how big the garden already is; if your mind drifts to the one thing you don't have, see it and come back to the list. If you pray, close it with alhamdulillah for the garden.
Khalifah, a steward trusted with one limit: a garden of everything given freely, where you will, except a single place not to go near.
Your line: everything, minus one. The yes comes first, and it is far bigger than the no. Twenty-five days in.

26.title: The whisper
26.hook: Shaytan whispers to them both and they eat, and their shame appears (7:20–22)
26.howItsDone: When Muslims feel an evil or anxious whisper, many say a'udhu billahi mina sh-shaytani r-rajim, I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan, and recite the last two surahs, al-Falaq and an-Nas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khalifah, and the garden's one tree. Everything given freely, and a single limit: everything, minus one. Day twenty-six.

It's two in the morning and you can't sleep. A voice in your head starts up. It never shouts. Just reasonable. One more episode won't hurt. You deserve that. Or the other kind: they were laughing at you, weren't they. You'll never be good enough. It sounds exactly like your own voice. That's what makes it work. Today, the garden has everything, and one tree, and then someone starts to talk. Not with a shout, or a threat. With a whisper.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `A REASONABLE LITTLE VOICE.` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE YOU.`

segments.voice: Surah seven, verse twenty: “Then Satan whispered to them.” The Arabic verb is waswasa, and listen to it: was-was. The word itself whispers. It's the sound of lips close to an ear. What did he say? He didn't say, disobey God. He renamed the tree. In another surah, he calls it the tree of immortality, and a kingdom that never wears out. Your Lord only forbade it, he says, so you wouldn't become angels, or live forever. Then he swore to them that he was a sincere adviser. The forbidden thing, dressed up as a gift. A limit, dressed up as God holding out on you. And they ate, and at once their shame appeared to them, and they began covering themselves with leaves of the garden. In surah seven, the whisper, the eating and the shame are all told in the Arabic dual: the two of them. The Qur'an doesn't pin it on the woman. The whisper came to both, and both ate. The Qur'an's last surah names this voice: in Pickthall's words, “the sneaking whisperer, Who whispereth in the hearts of mankind.” In Arabic, al-waswas al-khannas, the whisperer who slinks back. Many commentators explain: it retreats when God is remembered, and comes back when you forget. And a hadith in Bukhari brings real relief: God has forgiven people what their own souls whisper to them, as long as they don't act on it or say it. The whisper isn't the wrong. Following it is. So the thought at two in the morning isn't a verdict on you. It's just a voice. And not every voice is yours.
screen: `WASWAS — THE WORD WHISPERS.` · `HE RENAMED THE TREE.` · `THE WHISPER CAME TO BOTH.` · `THE WHISPERER WHO SLINKS BACK.` · then, large: `THEN SATAN WHISPERED TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Listen to your own mind; thoughts will come, some kind, some sharp, some selling you something. Don't argue with any of them, but when one pulls at you, a craving, a cruel line about yourself, a grudge, label it softly, whisper, and let it pass like a car going by outside. If you pray, you can say a'udhu billah, I seek refuge in God, the words Muslims use when a whisper comes.
Waswas. The whisper: a quiet voice that renames the tree and sounds like your own. The whisperer slinks back when God is remembered.
Your line: not every voice is yours. The story isn't over yet. See you tomorrow.

27.title: The words of return
27.hook: Adam receives words from his Lord and turns back, and is forgiven (2:37; 7:23)
27.howItsDone: Muslims make tawbah by stopping the wrong, regretting it, resolving not to return to it, and, where someone was harmed, putting it right; many recite Adam's words from 7:23 in their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: waswas, the whisper that renamed the tree. They ate, and their shame appeared. Not every voice is yours.

A mistake lands, and it's clearly yours. The stomach drop. Then the fork in the road. One way: explain. It wasn't really my fault. Anyone would have. The other way: three hard words. I was wrong. One is easier in the moment. The other is the one people say lets them breathe again afterward. Adam and his wife stand in the garden, covering themselves with leaves. This is their fork. And the story remembers someone else who stood at one too.
screen: `THE STOMACH DROP.` → `EXPLAIN IT, OR SAY I WAS WRONG.` → `ADAM'S FORK IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Remember Iblis. When he refused to bow and was sent out, whose fault did he say it was? In surah seven, he says to God: because You have sent me astray. He blamed God. Now Adam and his wife, in the same surah, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!” No excuse. No blaming the whisperer, or each other. Surah two tells what happened next: “Then Adam received from his Lord words (of revelation), and He relented toward him.” Some early commentators say those words were this very prayer: God gave Adam the words to come back with. The word for it is tawbah, from the root t-w-b, to turn back, to return. And the same root is used for God. One of His names is at-Tawwab, the One who keeps turning back toward the one who turns. The verse ends: “Lo! He is the Relenting, the Merciful.” So tawbah isn't groveling. It's two turns: you turn around, and find you're being turned toward. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim pictures it. A man loses his camel in the desert, with all his food and water on it, and lies down to die. He wakes, and it's standing there. God, the hadith says, is happier with a servant's tawbah than that man is with his camel. And Muslim teachers draw one more thing from this: Adam was forgiven, there and then. The human story, in Islam, starts with a mistake, and a return that worked.

If you pray, say sorry to God in your own words, as plainly as Adam did; if you don't, say it silently to the person you let down, or just to yourself: I was wrong. Then notice what it feels like to have turned around.
Tawbah. Turning back, repentance: you turn toward God, and find God turning toward you.
Your line: we wronged ourselves; forgive us. The way back is open from the start. That was day twenty-seven.

28.title: The two sons
28.hook: one brother's offering is accepted, the other kills him, and a crow shows him how to bury the body (5:27–31)
28.carry: one life is like all lives
28.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 5:32 to teach the sanctity of every human life, and it appears in sermons and statements against violence; the story of the two sons is taught as a warning about jealousy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawbah, turning back, and Adam's words: we wronged ourselves; forgive us. Day twenty-eight.

Sibling rivalry has its classics: who got the bigger slice, who Mom liked better, who got the car. All week, the first human story happened between God and the first two people: a steward announced, the names, the one who wouldn't bow, a garden with one tree, a whisper, and a way back. Now the story comes down to earth, and the very next thing it shows is a family. Two brothers. This time, the rivalry doesn't end in a slammed door. It ends in the first death in the human story.
screen: `WHO GOT THE BIGGER SLICE?` → `DOWN TO EARTH: A FAMILY.` → `TWO BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Surah five tells it, and calls them simply the two sons of Adam. It never names them; tradition calls them Qabil and Habil, Cain and Abel. Each brings an offering to God. One is accepted. The other isn't. And the one whose offering was refused says: I will kill you. His brother's answer, in Pickthall's words: “Allah accepteth only from those who ward off (evil).” It isn't about me. Look at your own heart. Even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine to kill you; I fear God. His brother kills him anyway. The killer stands over the body and doesn't know what to do. God sends a crow, scratching at the ground, to show him how to hide his brother's body. And he cries out: woe to me, can't I even be like this crow? And he's filled with regret. Right after this story comes a line addressed to the Children of Israel. Whoever kills a soul, except in justice, it's as if he killed all people, and in Pickthall's words, “whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.” Jewish readers will recognize a close teaching in the Mishnah. A hadith in Bukhari adds: for every unjust killing since, a share falls on that first son, because he was the first to do it. So the lesson of this first family is simple and enormous. One person is a whole world.
screen: `TWO OFFERINGS, ONE ACCEPTED.` · `I WON'T RAISE MY HAND.` · `A CROW, SCRATCHING THE GROUND.` · `ONE LIFE, ALL MANKIND.` · then, large: `ONE LIFE IS LIKE ALL LIVES.`

segments.voice: Let a jealousy come to mind, one you've carried for a while, toward a sibling, a friend, a colleague, someone who seemed to get what you wanted; don't push it away or feed it, just notice where it lives in your body. Then picture the other person as a whole world, with their own worries, their own sleepless nights, people who love them, and hold that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Habil, the brother whose offering was accepted and who told Qabil it isn't about me, look at your own heart, before the first death in the human story.
Your line: one life is like all lives. A week, done: day twenty-eight.
